chain.g: to keep, guard, look after, watch

ety.text: From Middle English kepen (“to keep, guard, look after, watch”), from Old English cēpan (“to seize, hold, observe”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōpijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōpijaną (“to look, heed, watch, observe”) (compare West Frisian kypje (“to look”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵab-, *ǵāb- (“to look after”) (compare Lithuanian žẽbti (“to eat reluctantly”), Russian забо́та (zabóta, “care, worry”)). The dialectal sense of the verb meaning “to put back” or “put away” may be analyzed as a semantic loan from a local language—compare Welsh cadw and Mandarin 收 (shōu).
From Middle English kepe, kep, from the verb (see above).

senses.d: To continue in (a course or mode of action); to not intermit or fall from; to uphold or maintain.
ex: to keep silence;  to keep possession

senses.d: To remain faithful to a given promise or word.
ex: to keep one's word;  to keep one's promise
Both day and night did we keep company.

senses.d: To maintain possession of.
ex: I keep a small stock of painkillers for emergencies.
I only meant to lend him the shirt at first, but it looked better on him than me, so I told him to keep it.

senses.d: To maintain the condition of; to preserve in a certain state.
ex: I keep my specimens under glass to protect them.
The abundance of squirrels kept the dogs running for hours.

senses.d: To record transactions, accounts, or events in.
ex: I used to keep a diary.

senses.d: To enter (accounts, records, etc.) in a book.
To remain in; to be confined to.
ex: The wrathful skies / Gallow the very wanderers of the dark / And make them keep their caves.

senses.d: To restrain.
ex: I keep my pet gerbil away from my brother.
Don't let me keep you; I know you have things to be doing.

senses.d: To watch over, look after, guard, protect.
ex: May the Lord keep you from harm.
cursse on thy cruell hond, / That twise hath sped; yet shall it not thee keepe / From the third brunt of this my fatall brond […]

senses.d: To supply with necessities and financially support (a person).
ex: He kept a mistress for over ten years.

senses.d: The main tower of a castle or fortress, located within the castle walls.
The food or money required to keep someone alive and healthy; one's support, maintenance.
ex: He works as a cobbler's apprentice for his keep.

senses.d: The state of being kept; hence, the resulting condition; case.
ex: to be in good keep

senses.d: A cap for holding something, such as a journal box, in place.
The act or office of keeping; custody; guard; care; heed; charge; notice.
ex: Pan, thou god of shepherds all, / Which of our tender lambkins takest keep.

senses.d: That which is kept in charge; a charge.
ex: Often he used of his keep / A sacrifice to bring.

senses.d: A mistress (the other woman in an extramarital relationship, generally including sexual relations).

chain.g: keen, fierce, bold, brave, warlike, powerful; learned, clever, wise

ety.text: From Middle English kene (“bold, brave, sharp”), from Old English cēne (“keen, fierce, bold, brave, warlike, powerful; learned, clever, wise”), from Proto-Germanic *kōniz (“knowledgeable, skilful, experienced, clever, capable”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).
From Irish caoin (“to lament, keen”).

senses.d: Often with a prepositional phrase, or with to and an infinitive: showing a quick and ardent responsiveness or willingness; eager, enthusiastic, interested.
ex: I’m keen on computers.
I’m keen on you.

senses.d: Fierce, intense, vehement.
ex: This boy has a keen appetite.
[N]euer did I know / A creature that did beare the ſhape of man / So keene and greedy to confound a man.

senses.d: Having a fine edge or point; sharp.
ex:
The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen
 As is the Razors edge, inuisible: […]

senses.d: Acute of mind, having or expressing mental acuteness; penetrating, sharp.
ex:
For when we rage, aduiſe is often ſeene
 By blunting vs to make our wits more keene.
So, when remote futurity is brought / Before the keen inquiry of her thought, / A terrible sagacity informs / The poet's heart; […]

senses.d: Acrimonious, bitter, piercing.
ex: keen satire or sarcasm

senses.d: Cutting, penetrating, piercing, sharp.
ex: a keen wind
the cold is very keen

senses.d: Of prices, extremely low as to be competitive.
Marvelous.
ex: I just got this peachy keen new dress.

senses.d: Brave, courageous; audacious, bold.
To make cold, to sharpen.
A prolonged wail for a deceased person.
To utter a keen.
To utter with a loud wailing voice or wordless cry.
ex: Pelicans fly below us with stiffly formal strokes, and gulls wheel and keen.
Satiran, lost in his own grief, shuddered once, then lifted his head to the sky and keened out his loss to the heavens.

senses.d: To mourn.
ex: She sniffed and nodded and cried and wailed and keened for her husband, who would never come back to her.

senses.d: One who keeps (retains) something.
ex: Finders keepers; losers weepers.

senses.d: One who remains or keeps in a place or position.
ex: discreet; chaste; keepers at home

senses.d: A fruit or vegetable that keeps (remains good) for some time without spoiling.
ex: Roxbury Russet: Market and keeper.

senses.d: A person or thing worth keeping.
ex: "Okay, that's a keeper," Harold said as he netted the 3-pounder and put him on a stringer over the side of the boat.
When he brought me home and volunteered to come with me while I walked my dog, Max, I knew he was a keeper.

senses.d: A person charged with guarding or caring for, storing, or maintaining something; a custodian, a guard; sometimes a gamekeeper.
ex: And the Lord said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?

senses.d: The player charged with guarding a goal or wicket; a goalkeeper or wicketkeeper.
At Eton College, a student who is the captain of a sport or an activity such as drama.
A part of a mechanism that catches or retains another part, for example the part of a door lock that fits in the frame and receives the bolt.
A thin, flexible tress or tongue of material (e.g. leather) at the end of a crop opposite the handle, which is broad enough to prevent the horse's skin from being marked as it might be by a whip.
ex: The all-whalebone crop, braided with gut, pigskin handle, single brown stitched leather keeper, and close[…]

senses.d: An offensive play in which the quarterback runs toward the goal with the ball after it is snapped.
